sections.h2: How does property tax work in New York?
sections.html:
New York property tax is assessed and collected locally, so the person you pay and the dates you follow depend on the county, city, town, village and school district where the house sits. State law sets the common rules for challenging an assessment, claiming relief and handling delinquent taxes. The local assessor and the local collecting office supply the numbers.

Who enforces unpaid tax also varies. Under Real Property Tax Law section 1102, the enforcing officer is the county treasurer or commissioner of finance where the county is the tax district, the official named in the charter in a city, the village treasurer in a village, and the town supervisor in a town, unless another law says otherwise.

Owners who plan to sell should find out early which office holds the current bill and any unpaid balance. The title company will ask the same office for a payoff figure before closing.

sections.h2: How do I challenge my New York property assessment?
sections.html:
File a complaint with the assessor before the Board of Assessment Review hears complaints, or with the board itself at the hearing. Under section 524, a complaint cannot be filed at an adjourned hearing, and anything filed on or before the hearing date is timely.

The board starts hearing complaints on the fourth Tuesday of May, unless a charter, county tax act or special law sets another date. Section 512 also lets an assessing unit that shares an assessor with another unit adopt a local law moving the first hearing date no earlier than the fourth Tuesday of May and no later than the second Tuesday of June.

Three points shape a strong complaint:

  • The legal grounds are that the assessment is excessive, unequal or unlawful, or that the property is misclassified.
  • Outside cities of five million or more, the complaint goes on the commissioner's prescribed form, with a statement of the reduction sought and an estimate of the property's value.
  • If the assessor and the owner both sign the statement on the form, it becomes a stipulation to the assessed value. When that figure is entered on the final roll, the owner gives up court review under Article 7.

Where a town or city raises an assessment, section 510 requires a mailed notice, sent no sooner than 120 days before the tentative roll is due and no later than ten days before the hearing. The notice must list the board's meeting dates. A missed mailing does not stop the tax from being levied. New York City follows its own charter on notices.

sections.h2: What if the board does not lower the assessment?
sections.html:
An owner can ask the Supreme Court to review it, but the clock is short. Section 702 requires the proceeding to start within thirty days after the final assessment roll is completed and filed, and a late petition is a complete defense that ends the case.

The roll is not considered finally completed until the last day the law sets for filing it or until notice has been given as required, whichever comes later. Because the thirty days are counted from that date, ask the assessor's office for the roll filing date rather than guessing from the hearing date.

A seller who is mid-contract should tell the closing attorney about any pending complaint or court filing.

sections.h2: What is STAR and who qualifies?
sections.html:
STAR is the state's school tax relief program for owner-occupied primary residences. The Department of Taxation and Finance describes two versions on its Types of STAR page, updated October 27, 2026.

New York STAR benefit types (source: NYS Department of Taxation and Finance, Types of STAR)
BenefitWho it servesIncome limitValue basis
Basic STAROwner-occupied primary residences$500,000 for the credit, $250,000 for the exemptionFirst $30,000 of full value
Enhanced STARPrimary residences of owners age 65 and older$110,750 or less for 2026-2027, $113,550 or less for 2027-2028First $91,700 of full value for 2027-2028

The benefit reduces school district taxes only. It does not touch county, town or city bills, except in New York City, Buffalo, Rochester, Yonkers and Syracuse, where the exemption is applied partly to city taxes and partly to school taxes. Seniors who receive STAR may also qualify for the senior citizens exemption.

sections.h2: How do I register for STAR after buying or selling?
sections.html:
Register once through the Homeowner Benefit Portal in your Individual Online Services account. The Tax Department then issues the STAR credit each year for as long as you remain eligible, according to its STAR registration page.

A new owner should register as soon as the house becomes the primary residence. The registration form asks for these items:

  • names and Social Security numbers for all owners and their spouses;
  • the school district and the approximate purchase date;
  • the sellers' names, which are optional but may help the credit arrive before school taxes are due;
  • the most recent school tax bill, if the current owners received one;
  • the legal name of any trust that holds title;
  • federal or state income tax returns for all owners.

The same portal lets an owner edit or close a registration, which is the step a seller takes after the house is gone. Enrolling in direct deposit and switching from the exemption to the credit are also handled there.

sections.h2: Is there a senior citizen exemption in New York?
sections.html:
Yes, but a municipality has to choose to offer it. Real Property Tax Law section 467 lets a local governing board, after a public hearing, adopt a law exempting up to 50 percent of the assessed value of property owned by people 65 and older. The statute also covers a married couple or siblings when one of them is 65 or older.

The exemption scales down as income rises, and municipalities can raise the income ceiling by local law. Because each county, city, town and school district decides separately, ask the local assessor whether the exemption is offered, what the income cap is, and when the application is due. Do not assume the neighboring town follows the same rules.

sections.h2: What happens if New York property tax goes unpaid?
sections.html:
The unpaid tax becomes a delinquent tax lien, and the owner can redeem the property by paying the enforcing officer the lien amount plus lawful charges. Under section 1110, the redemption period ends two years after the lien date.

That two-year period can change in three ways:

  • A tax district may lengthen it for residential or farm property.
  • A district may shorten it to one year for residential property placed on a vacant and abandoned list before the taxes went delinquent.
  • A published foreclosure notice may name a later expiration date, and then that date controls.

Charges are part of the delinquent tax. Section 1102 counts interest, penalties, notice and publication costs, and recording costs among them. It treats up to $250 per parcel, or 2 percent of the taxes, interest and penalties due, whichever is greater, as a reasonable foreclosure-related charge without further proof. After redemption, the enforcing officer will issue a certificate of redemption on request, and filing it with the county clerk cancels the notice of pendency for that parcel.

sections.h2: Can I sell a New York house with property tax due?
sections.html:
The statute lets a parcel be redeemed by paying the enforcing officer the lien amount plus charges, so the payoff has to reach that office before the redemption period ends. A sale gives the owner a way to do that, with the title company sending the payoff from the proceeds.

Order the figure early and get it in writing. A deed given in connection with a tax sale is a nontaxable conveyance under the state transfer tax rules, according to the Tax Department's real estate transfer tax page.

Ask the county treasurer, the city finance office, or the town or village tax office for the payoff and the redemption deadline. If the deadline is close, share it with the buyer at the start so the closing date works around it.

faqs.q: When is Grievance Day in New York?
faqs.a: It is usually the fourth Tuesday of May, when the Board of Assessment Review begins hearing complaints. A charter, county tax act or special law can set a different date, and some assessing units that share an assessor may move it to as late as the second Tuesday of June. Confirm the date with your assessor.

faqs.q: Does STAR lower my county or town tax?
faqs.a: No, STAR applies only to school district taxes. The exception is New York City, Buffalo, Rochester, Yonkers and Syracuse, where the benefit is applied partly to city taxes and partly to school taxes. County and town bills are not reduced in other places.

faqs.q: How long can I wait to redeem after a tax lien in New York?
faqs.a: The standard redemption period is two years after the lien date. A tax district can lengthen it for residential property, shorten it to one year for vacant and abandoned residential property, or publish a later date in its notice. Ask the enforcing officer for the date that applies to your parcel.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to sue over an assessment in New York?
faqs.a: A court proceeding to review an assessment must start within thirty days after the final assessment roll is completed and filed. Signing a stipulation with the assessor on the complaint form ends court review for that year. Talk to a New York attorney about the exact date before it passes.

faqs.q: Do I need to tell STAR when I sell my house?
faqs.a: Yes, close or update the registration in the Homeowner Benefit Portal after the sale. The buyer registers separately once the house becomes their primary residence. Giving the buyer the sellers' names on the form can help the credit arrive before school taxes are due.
